params.body:
Nothing counted a car being looked at. The page counter from 25 September knows which *screen* was opened, which is a question about the platform; on the marketplace it knew the route and not the vehicle, and in a dealer's own website widget it counted nothing at all, because the visitor there is not signed in.

So the one question a dealer actually has — how often is my stock being looked at — had no answer on either side. Three changes.

## 1. A photo is not a screen

`RecordPageView` promised in its own docblock to count "a successful HTML response". It never checked. The first day of counting showed the bill: of the eight busiest routes, three were photo routes (`website.index.image`, `ownvehicle.index.image`, `dealer.index.image`), together **732 of the 1,166 views**. The measure called "screens opened" was mostly a photo counter — the mistake R P3-16.3 names for handlings, made again one table further on.

Two checks now, each for something different. The content type keeps out what is not HTML: a JPEG on a named route answering 200 passed every other filter. The opening of the document keeps out what is HTML but not a page: modals and infinite-scroll slices, which are answers to a screen the reader already had open.

## 2. Cars, not screens

`vehicle_views`: one row per day, car and side, with the count. The side (`platform` or `embed`) stays in the row rather than being added away — a signed-in dealer on the marketplace is trade, a visitor in the widget is a customer. Added up they answer whether more is being looked at; only apart do they say where it moved.

The garage on the row is the one that **owns** the car, not the one looking: a dealer asks about their own stock, and on the marketplace those two differ.

Counting happens in one middleware rather than in the three controllers, for the reason the architecture paper gives about `Project::fromPortal()`: a step you have to remember gets forgotten, and a fourth screen showing a car would silently not be counted. A detail loaded into a modal does count here, unlike in the page counter — the question is whether the car was looked at, not whether a document was loaded.

A view of a car that does not exist writes nothing: the insert reads `vehicles` in the same statement, so a bot walking made-up ids leaves no rows.

## 3. The widget, without knowing the visitor

The embed routes are public and crawled as ordinary traffic — on 20 September Amazonbot asked for `/website/detail/ODM2OQ==`. A counter that takes crawlers along is a crawler counter, and would report a car getting busier in the week a bot walked the sitemap. `Crawlers::isMachine()` tests the user agent, which is all a public request offers; a request with no user agent counts as a machine, because a person wrongly skipped costs one view and a bot wrongly counted spoils the trend. It is not airtight, and the screen says so.

No ip, no cookie, no fingerprint, no `user_id` — the same line R P3-16.9 drew, and it holds harder here, because these are the customers of our customer. A test asserts those columns are absent, so adding one later is a deliberate act rather than a slip.

`embed_views` counts the widget being opened, per garage per day. That is the denominator: without it, "more cars are being looked at" cannot be told apart from "more people came to the dealer's website", and those call for opposite conclusions.

## On the screen

Three measures join the four that were there — cars on the platform, cars on the dealer site, widget opened — and inherit the whole frame: the comparison with the period before, the series, the garage table, the day they started, and the admission that a daily total knows no hour. Labels in four languages, plus a footnote saying what these counters do not see.

`Activity::CACHE_KEY` gains a version. The facts array is the view's data, so its shape is part of the key: without this, five minutes of cached arrays from the previous version would meet a blade that reads a key they do not carry. The blade also falls back to nothing, so a missing number drops a sentence rather than a screen.

## Verified

`AViewIsACarBeingLookedAtTest` (16 tests) pins the shape and the middleware: that the two sides stay apart, that the garage is the owner, that an unknown side is refused, that a crawler and a mangled address leave nothing, that no visitor column exists, and — the one that would rot quietest — that every route name and parameter in the map is one the application still registers. Three tests in `CountingPagesWithoutCountingPeopleTest` cover the photo, the fragment and the whole document.

New rules R P3-16.17, R P3-16.18, R P3-16.19. `phpstan` green, `npm run build` green, `pint` green on the added files. Local suite: the same nine failures as on a clean `main` in my environment.

## Not in here

The numbers exist from the day this deploys and not before, so the before-and-after this was asked for starts accruing now. And a dealer cannot see their own car's count yet — `VehicleViews::forVehicle()` is there and nothing calls it. That is the next thing worth building, and it is a product feature rather than analytics.
params.title: Count a car being looked at, on both sides
